title_original: The Memory of Things: Sonia Gomes and the Art of Transformation
excerpt_original: At the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, Brazilian artist Sonia Gomes explores the emotional lives of discarded textiles, the cultural traditions of Minas Gerais and the freedom of making in her solo exhibition, Wild Heart. […]

blocks.text: At the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, Brazilian artist Sonia Gomes explores the emotional lives of discarded textiles, the cultural traditions of Minas Gerais and the freedom of making in her solo exhibition, Wild Heart .

A wedding dress once worn by someone’s grandmother, a scarf carried across continents, a piece of fabric bearing the marks of an unknown life. In the hands of Brazilian artist Sonia Gomes, these seemingly ordinary materials become sculptural forms that resist easy classification. Twisted, knotted, stitched and suspended, they carry fragments of their former existence while taking on new identities through an intuitive process of transformation. Sonia Gomes, Pano ( Pano series), 2012. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, Pano ( Pano series), 2012. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.text: At the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, Wild Heart , curated by Daria de Beauvais, brings together works that reveal Gomes’s deeply personal relationship with material, memory and artistic freedom. Drawing on the cultural traditions of Minas Gerais, where she grew up, her practice draws inspiration from the colours, rhythms, and ceremonial expressions of Brazilian popular culture. References to ancestral knowledge, religious celebrations, and collective rituals emerge in compositions that occupy the space between sculpture, painting, and textile art.

Taking its title from a work inspired by Clarice Lispector’s novel Near to the Wild Heart , the exhibition considers freedom not simply as a theme but as a way of working. For Gomes, materials are not passive objects waiting to be transformed. They possess their own histories, textures and possibilities, guiding the artist through a process she describes as listening.

In conversation with ART AFRICA , Gomes reflects on the intimate histories embedded in textiles, the influence of Afro-Brazilian cultural traditions, and the importance of letting materials determine their own forms. She also discusses her first major institutional exhibition in Paris and her ambition to establish an institute supporting emerging artists. Sonia Gomes, Magia (Pano series), 2014. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, Magia (Pano series), 2014. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.text: ART AFRICA : The title Wild Heart suggests something instinctive, untamed, and deeply personal. What does this title mean to you, and how does it relate to the works in the exhibition?

Sonia Gomes: One work in the exhibition is titled Perto do Coração Selvagem (Near to the Wild Heart), after Clarice Lispector’s book. In the book, the wild heart is free, and this idea deeply inspired me. The curator Daria de Beauvais then chose the exhibition title ‘Wild Hear t’ because she felt it captured the spirit of my work well. Sonia Gomes, untitled (Raiz series), 2018. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings on wood. Collection Örneberg Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, untitled (Raiz series), 2018. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings on wood. Collection Örneberg Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.text: Your practice transforms found and gifted textiles into sculptural forms, each carrying traces of its past. How do you approach the histories in these materials, and what guides their transformation into new works?

Each work begins with necessity and intuition. I work with materials I receive, including clothing, bedspreads, towels, and embroidery from different parts of the world. I respect the materiality and history of every piece that comes to me, whether it is a wedding dress that belonged to someone’s grandmother or scarves worn on journeys. These materials carry anonymous yet deeply intimate memories and emotions.

Throughout my process, however, these materials become something else. It is a constant exercise in free experimentation, in which I twist, sew, and tie the materials onto metal or wooden structures to create something new. The work will always retain something of what the material once represented, but it becomes something else: an object, an installation, a sculpture, or a painting. Sonia Gomes, untitled (Torção series), 2013. Fabrics, stitching and bindings on wire. Collection particulière, Londres. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, untitled (Torção series), 2013. Fabrics, stitching and bindings on wire. Collection particulière, Londres. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.text: Your sculptures often take on organic, almost living forms through knotting, twisting, weaving, and assembling. How does your relationship with the materials shape the forms that emerge in your creative process?
My work has an organic, intuitive character. I use branches, tree trunks, and reclaimed wood as canvases or surfaces on which I paint and sew, creating new works.

My relationship with the materials is one of listening. The material itself guides the form. As I mentioned earlier, my entire working process begins with feeling. The material tells me what to do, and the work changes according to its shape. It is a process of observing and sensing what each element offers to the composition.

This process of listening to the material indicates where it wants to go and what it wants to become. For me, it is an intimate process of engaging with the substance of things. I feel their volume, texture, weight, colour, and so on. Sonia Gomes, Torção ( Torção series), 2004. Fabrics and wire. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © Edouard Fraipont.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, Torção ( Torção series), 2004. Fabrics and wire. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © Edouard Fraipont.

blocks.text: Your work draws on your Afro-Brazilian heritage and traditions of making passed down through generations. How have these cultural histories shaped your artistic language, and how do they continue to inform your practice today?

My work engages with the traditions and artistic expressions of the interior of Minas Gerais, where the visual aesthetic, shaped by rhythm, colours, and architecture, has deeply nourished and continues to nourish me.

This heritage comes from the world and from my experience of living in it. The Brazilian people are incredibly diverse, as are our traditions, and I have had the opportunity to experience some of them firsthand.

I feel there is an ancestral heritage behind what I do, and that my work touches on elements of our culture with African roots. As Brazilians, however, we have developed our own ways of preserving this history through traditional celebrations, religious practices, and family customs. Sonia Gomes, Tereza , 2021-2025. Fabrics, laces, stitching and binding on ropes. Courtesy of the artis and Pace Gallery (New York, Los Angeles, Londres, Geneva, Berlin, Séoul, Tokyo). Photo © Damian Griffiths.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, Tereza , 2021-2025. Fabrics, laces, stitching and binding on ropes. Courtesy of the artis and Pace Gallery (New York, Los Angeles, Londres, Geneva, Berlin, Séoul, Tokyo). Photo © Damian Griffiths.

blocks.text: Wild Heart brings together memory, identity, and cultural transmission. How do you understand the relationship between personal experience and collective history in your work?

Wild Heart includes a series titled Estandarte (Banner), which presents itself as a presence. My reference for this series was the Folia de Reis and Reinado celebrations in Minas Gerais, where banners guide the collective.

In Brazilian popular festivals, these objects function as markers of place and as announcements of what is to come. In this way, the series invites viewers to follow its rhythms, textures, and compositions. Sonia Gomes, Perto do Coração Sel-vagem (Trouxa series), 2025. Fabrics, laces,ropes, stitching, bindings and beads. Courtesy of the artistand Pace (New York, Los Angeles, Londres, Genève, Berlin, Séoul, Tokyo)

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, Perto do Coração Sel-vagem (Trouxa series), 2025. Fabrics, laces,ropes, stitching, bindings and beads. Courtesy of the artistand Pace (New York, Los Angeles, Londres, Genève, Berlin, Séoul, Tokyo)

blocks.text: Colour plays an important role in your practice, with red appearing throughout the exhibition. How do you approach colour as a material and expressive element, and what significance does it hold in the works presented?

In my work, colour engages with the traditions and artistic expressions of interior Minas Gerais, where I experienced popular culture in all its diversity and intensity. Alongside music, colour is a prominent element in these artistic expressions. The clothing, ribbons, and vivid forms of this culture resonate unconsciously in my creative process. Sonia Gomes, Aninhado , 2019. Fabrics, ropes, bindings, metal cage and wood. Collection Flavia NespattiCourtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York). Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, Aninhado , 2019. Fabrics, ropes, bindings, metal cage and wood. Collection Flavia NespattiCourtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York). Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.text: Your practice engages with histories of colonisation, race and gender through materials and techniques often associated with domestic labour and craft. How do you understand the relationship between these histories and the artistic processes you employ?
This is your interpretation of my practice as engaging with these histories. My work is open to interpretation, so it is perfectly fine for you to approach it this way.

My work is intuitive, sensory, and empirical. It comes from my roots, my ancestry, and my history, as well as the marks left by time, which I find deeply interesting. Through my work, I create a new history. I work out of a need to create, and the work transcends that need. All artistic work is, in itself, transcendent. Sonia Gomes, O Olho Que Tudo Vê, 2019. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings. Collection particulière. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.caption: Sonia Gomes, O Olho Que Tudo Vê, 2019. Fabrics, laces, stitching and bindings. Collection particulière. Courtesy of the artist and Mendes Wood DM (São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York) Photo © EstudioEmObra.

blocks.text: Presented to audiences at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris, how do you approach your work in this new cultural and institutional context, and what possibilities does this exhibition open for your ongoing artistic exploration?
I need to be here, at my first major institutional exhibition in Paris. The Palais de Tokyo’s experimental approach strongly resonates with my own practice.
This context also connects with my plans to create an institute with similar characteristics, dedicated to supporting emerging artists at the beginning of their careers.

My work unfolds intuitively throughout the creative process, and being part of an institution that embraces experimentation provides a meaningful context for this approach. It also offers an opportunity to continue developing my artistic research in an environment that is open to new possibilities.
This exhibition is on view at the Palais de Tokyo in Paris until 14 February 2027.
